rationale: A wins because it keeps the dangerous tensions as testable reporting questions instead of dressing one company’s messy quarter up as a category thesis. A’s “Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product while closing a US plant” has a wording problem, but the body correctly asks whether this is “a category correction or a company-specific turnaround.” B blows the safer lane with “Plant-based dairy's growth era is over,” which is a grand sector claim built on one company update and a hope that someone else brings the evidence. That is how a decent pitch walks itself into a reporter’s delete pile wearing a fake mustache.
gaps_in_A: “Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product” is not supported. The update says 31% lower than the previous formula, not lowest in Oatly’s portfolio.
“evidence the user can cite for the green-premium belief” is the right proof ask, but without it the shelf-price angle is still more premise than story.
The labor angle is useful risk prep, but “What happens to the workers” cannot become outreach until the plant location, headcount, closure date, and severance facts exist.
gaps_in_B: “Plant-based dairy's growth era is over” is an invented category conclusion. The set admits it needs category data, then lets the headline overclaim anyway.

“closing a plant and cutting its carbon footprint in the same quarter” is too tidy. The update says the operating-loss context was last quarter; the plant closure and rollout are current, but “same quarter” is not established.
“the 31% number is unpitchable without it — it's the load-bearing fact in three of four angles” exposes the duplication problem. Too much of B depends on the same LCA claim wearing different jackets.
The first angle lists “no price change at retail” under facts even while warning that retail price does not answer café surcharge. Good catch, messy grounding.
